doc.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: What he thinks about while improvising
summary: He says thinking and improvising are incompatible, and discusses singing along with solos (Armstrong, Garner, Albert Collins).

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Speaking of exposed, I was watching you play.

I was watching you play on that video and trying to imagine what’s going on in your head. Because you were playing “Body and Soul” and I think you started with the bridge as a matter of fact, or it was almost like you played the bridge as an intro.
So I’m going to assume that was done on the spot?
Okay. But then — I’ll shorten the question. Can you tell me what you’re thinking about when you’re improvising?

Those two are dichotomous. It’s like can you tell me what you’re thinking about when you’re making love to your wife? Well if you’re thinking about anything it’s like that’s totally not part of the process. Same thing with improvising. I mean the idea is to just let your inner voice take over. I mean, and you know, some people sing along with their solos. I’m not a big fan of that because I think that kind of locks you into —

Yeah. But great musicians such as Louis Armstrong could play anything they could sing and they could sing anything they could play you know. Erroll Gardner used to sing [moans]. I have a great DAT recording of Albert Collins doing a guitar solo, but the amp is in another room. It’s just a microphone, his talk-back microphone and you can hear his strings going — you can hear acoustically his strings, but he’s going [moans] it sounds like a demonic possession. It’s unbelievable. I’m sorry. I’m digressing again.
